questions.question: Which statement about the legal status of this FDA aseptic processing guidance is correct?

options.A: It does not establish legally enforceable responsibilities and represents only FDA's current thinking; "should" means a recommendation unless specific regulations are cited
options.B: It replaces the provisions of 21 CFR 210/211 on aseptic processing and carries the same enforceable force as regulation
options.C: It is binding only on biological products submitted under a BLA; NDA and ANDA products may decide for themselves whether to follow it
options.D: It is effective in parallel with the 1987 Aseptic Processing Guideline, and both documents are enforceable

questions.explanation: Guidance does not establish legally enforceable responsibilities and describes only FDA's current thinking; "should" in the text means a recommendation, and only the cited CFR provisions are requirements. It helps in complying with 21 CFR 210/211 and does not replace them; it applies to NDAs, ANDAs, and BLAs; and it has superseded the 1987 guideline rather than running in parallel with it.

questions.question: Biological products are subject to both 21 CFR 600-680 and 21 CFR 210/211. How should a case be handled if both cannot be complied with at the same time?

options.A: Always follow 210/211, because 210/211 is the focus of this guidance
options.B: Follow the regulation specifically applicable to the product, which supersedes the more general provision
options.C: Follow the stricter of the two provisions, regardless of which part of the regulations it is in
options.D: The manufacturer may choose either one, as long as the rationale is documented in an SOP and approved by QA

questions.explanation: Under 21 CFR 210.2 and 211.1, when 600-680 and 210/211 cannot both be complied with, the regulation specifically applicable to the product supersedes the more general regulation. The principle is that the specific provision prevails, not "the stricter one," and it is neither always 210/211 nor left to the manufacturer's choice.

questions.question: Why does the guidance regard the contamination risk of aseptic processing as higher than that of terminal sterilization?

options.A: The raw materials and containers used in aseptic processing usually have much higher bioburden than those of terminally sterilized products, so the sterilization load is heavier
options.B: Terminally sterilized products need not be filled in a high-quality environment, so facility controls are simpler
options.C: The components are sterilized separately and then assembled, there is no sterilization step in the final container, and any manipulation during assembly can introduce contamination
options.D: Aseptic processing has fewer variables than terminal sterilization, but any one that goes wrong has a greater impact

questions.explanation: In aseptic processing, the drug product, containers, and closures are sterilized separately (for example, vials by dry heat, stoppers by moist heat, and the drug solution by filtration) and then assembled; there is no sterilization step in the final container, so any manual or mechanical manipulation before or during assembly carries a contamination risk. The document says aseptic processing has more variables than terminal sterilization, not fewer; terminally sterilized products are also filled in a high-quality environment and simply have a sterilization step afterward; and the bioburden of raw materials is not a reason the document gives.

questions.question: According to the guidance, when should aseptic processing be chosen to manufacture a sterile drug product?

options.A: Aseptic processing is always used for biological or protein drug products
options.B: It is left to the manufacturer to choose based on cost and capacity, because the two approaches are completely equivalent under the regulations
options.C: Aseptic processing is preferred even when terminal sterilization is feasible, because the product suffers less heat degradation
options.D: Only when terminal sterilization is not feasible; where a special package offers significant advantages, adjunct steps may be added to improve sterility assurance

questions.explanation: The recognized principle is to use aseptic processing only when terminal sterilization is not feasible. If certain final packages (such as some dual-chamber syringes) have unique advantages that terminal sterilization cannot deliver, manufacturers may consider adding adjunct processing steps to improve sterility assurance. The document does not say that biologics always use aseptic processing, nor that the two are equivalent or may be chosen on cost.

questions.question: Which statement about the scope of this guidance is correct?

options.A: It fully covers every step of upstream bulk processing, with only a brief treatment of the finished product side
options.B: It discusses sterilization of components, containers, and closures, but not terminal sterilization of the drug product itself
options.C: It discusses only isolator systems, and conventional cleanrooms are addressed in the 1987 guideline
options.D: It covers all aspects of aseptic processing and also includes validation requirements for terminal sterilization processes

questions.explanation: The Scope states that the document discusses only some topics, focusing on CGMP for finished products and giving only limited information on upstream bulk processing; it discusses sterilization of components, containers, and closures but not terminal sterilization of the drug product. Isolators are just one of the topics discussed, conventional cleanrooms remain the main subject, and the 1987 guideline has been superseded.

questions.question: Which statement about the airborne particle standard and measurement method for the critical area (Class 100 / ISO 5) is correct?

options.A: No more than 3,520 particles of ≥0.5 µm per cubic meter, measured at rest in the center of the room
options.B: No more than 35,200 particles of ≥0.5 µm per cubic meter, measured within 1 meter of the work site
options.C: No more than 3,520 particles of ≥0.5 µm per cubic meter, measured during filling, typically not more than 1 foot from the work site
options.D: No more than 352,000 particles of ≥0.5 µm per cubic meter, measured once at rest before the start of each shift

questions.explanation: The critical area is near the exposed sterilized containers and the filling/closing operations; it allows no more than 3,520 particles of ≥0.5 µm per cubic meter, measured in the airflow, typically not more than 1 foot from the work site, and during filling/closing operations (dynamic). 35,200 is ISO 6 and 352,000 is ISO 7; measuring at rest or only before a shift does not comply, and the document also recommends routine monitoring every shift.

questions.question: What minimum classification does FDA recommend for the area immediately adjacent to the aseptic filling line?

options.A: At least Class 10,000 (ISO 7) under dynamic conditions
options.B: At least Class 100,000 (ISO 8) under static conditions
options.C: The entire filling room must be Class 100 (ISO 5)
options.D: At least Class 1,000 (ISO 6) under dynamic conditions

questions.explanation: FDA recommends that the area immediately adjacent to the aseptic filling line be at least Class 10,000 (ISO 7) under dynamic conditions. Manufacturers may also classify it as ISO 6 or maintain the entire filling room at ISO 5, but those are options and not the minimum requirement. ISO 8 applies to less critical activities (such as equipment washing).

questions.question: An aseptic processing room in a facility directly adjoins an unclassified room. According to the guidance, how should the pressure differential be managed?

options.A: A positive pressure of about 5 Pa with the door closed is enough, with no special control when the door is open
options.B: Because the unclassified room has more particles, the aseptic processing room should be kept at negative pressure relative to it, to avoid pushing particles toward the filling line
options.C: Measuring and recording the differential once at the start of each shift is enough, with no need for continuous monitoring or alarms
options.D: A significant positive pressure (for example, at least 12.5 Pa) should be maintained at all times; if it falls below the limit, it must be restored and the environmental quality confirmed

questions.explanation: Where an aseptic processing room adjoins an unclassified room, a significant positive pressure (for example, at least 12.5 Pa) should be maintained at all times; if the differential falls below the limit, it must be restored and the environmental quality of the aseptic processing room confirmed. Between adjacent rooms of different classification (doors closed) the differential is generally at least 10-15 Pa, and outward airflow and door-open time must be controlled when doors are open. Pressure differentials should be monitored continuously every shift and recorded frequently, alarms should be documented, and deviations investigated.

questions.question: In an in-situ leak test of a HEPA filter, at what fraction of the upstream challenge concentration does a single probe reading count as a significant leak?

options.A: 0.1%, requiring the filter to be replaced at the next annual maintenance
options.B: 0.01%, requiring the filter to be replaced or locally repaired and then retested
options.C: 0.03%, corresponding to the 99.97% efficiency specification
options.D: 1%, with anything below it an acceptable background value

questions.explanation: A single probe reading equivalent to 0.01% of the upstream challenge concentration indicates a significant leak; the HEPA should be replaced or, where appropriate, locally repaired, and the repaired area must be retested for confirmation. 99.97% is the efficiency test specification used to grade the filter, not the leak test criterion. The document gives HEPA leak testing in aseptic processing rooms at twice a year as an example, and does not wait for annual maintenance.

questions.question: What is the difference between the leak test and the efficiency test of a HEPA filter?

options.A: The efficiency test grades the filter media with a monodisperse 0.3 µm aerosol; the leak test uses a polydisperse aerosol to scan the filter face and frame in situ
options.B: The methods are the same, differing only in that the efficiency test is done once a year and the leak test twice a year, both by the vendor
options.C: The efficiency test is done in situ after installation, and the leak test is done by the filter manufacturer before shipment
options.D: The leak test needs to measure only the downstream particle concentration, with no challenge aerosol added upstream, so it is easier to perform

questions.explanation: The efficiency test uses a monodisperse 0.3 µm aerosol to evaluate the filter media; the reading is an average over the whole filter face and is used to grade the filter, not to find leaks. The leak test uses a submicron polydisperse aerosol (with sufficient particles around 0.3 µm), and a photometer probe scans the entire filter face and frame in situ to find leaks in the media, frame, or seals. Without a sufficient upstream challenge, leaks cannot be detected.

questions.question: Which statement about monitoring the glove surfaces of aseptic operators complies with the guidance?

options.A: Sample each operator's gloves once a week, with other body sites sampled only during media fills
options.B: Wipe the gloves with a disinfectant before sampling to avoid environmental false positives affecting trend interpretation
options.C: Sample only operators who have had an excursion, with annual gowning requalification substituting for everyone else
options.D: Sample each operator's gloves every day or every batch, and do not disinfect the gloves before sampling

questions.explanation: Personnel monitoring should include surface samples of each operator's gloves every day or every batch, with sampling at an appropriate frequency of other strategically selected sites of the gown. Disinfecting gloves before sampling is inappropriate because it prevents microorganisms present during the operation from being recovered. For labor-intensive operations, QC should also establish a more thorough monitoring program.

questions.question: According to the guidance, under what circumstances is "once a year" gowning requalification generally sufficient?

options.A: For all aseptic operations, always once a year, with no adjustment according to circumstances
options.B: Once every three years after passing the initial gowning qualification
options.C: When operations are automated, with little personnel intervention, and monitoring data show the environment to be in control
options.D: For manual filling lines, because the operators' movements have already been assessed in media fills

questions.explanation: Annual requalification is generally sufficient provided that the operation is automated, personnel intervention is minimal, and monitoring data show the environment to be in control. Any aseptic operation with adverse conditions may need more or more frequent requalification. Manual filling lines carry higher risk and are not a situation where annual requalification is sufficient.

questions.question: When validating a depyrogenation process for containers and closures with an endotoxin spike, by how much should the data show endotoxin is reduced, at a minimum?

options.A: At least 99.9% (3 logs)
options.B: At least 99.9999% (6 logs)
options.C: At least 99% (2 logs)
options.D: At least 12 logs (overkill)

questions.explanation: Depyrogenation validation data should demonstrate that the process reduces endotoxin by at least 99.9% (3 logs), with a positive control used to measure the recovery of the method. If dry heat has been successfully validated to this level with an endotoxin challenge, validating sterilization with a BI is not additionally needed. 6 logs is a number associated with SAL or decontamination, and 12 logs is the definition of overkill sterilization; neither is a depyrogenation standard.

questions.question: How can endotoxin on equipment surfaces be dealt with?

options.A: Filtering the drug solution through a 0.2 µm sterilizing-grade filter removes it
options.B: Inactivation by high-temperature dry heat, or removal from the surface by cleaning procedures
options.C: Extending the hold time of moist heat sterilization (autoclave or SIP) is sufficient
options.D: Two sterilizing filters in series (redundant filtration) remove it

questions.explanation: The document points out that neither sterilizing-grade filters nor moist heat sterilization have been shown to remove endotoxin. Endotoxin on equipment surfaces can be inactivated by high-temperature dry heat or removed by cleaning procedures (for example, CIP with high-purity water or detergent rinses, finishing with a hot WFI rinse). After cleaning, equipment should be dried unless it goes straight into a sterilization step.

questions.question: When sterilization/depyrogenation of containers and closures is outsourced to a contract facility, what is the drug manufacturer's responsibility?

options.A: The contractor bears all responsibility, and the manufacturer need only state the quality requirements in the contract
options.B: The manufacturer must repeat full sterilization validation and endotoxin testing on every lot of containers and closures before accepting them for use
options.C: Review the contractor's validation protocols and reports; once the supplier's results have been periodically confirmed as reliable, lots can be accepted on the basis of the CoA
options.D: As long as the contractor holds ISO certification, review of validation documents can be waived

questions.explanation: A contractor that sterilizes or depyrogenates containers and closures is subject to the same CGMP as in-house processing. The drug manufacturer should review and evaluate the contractor's validation protocols and final validation reports; under 21 CFR 211.84, after confirming the reliability of the supplier's test results at appropriate intervals, material can be accepted on the basis of visual identification and review of the CoA. Responsibility is not transferred, and neither full retesting of every lot nor ISO certification removes the need for review.

questions.question: Why should an upper limit be set on the total filtration time of a drug solution?

options.A: Mainly for capacity planning, so that the filling schedule of each batch is predictable
options.B: To prevent microorganisms from penetrating the filter and to avoid a significant increase in upstream bioburden and endotoxin
options.C: Regulations require that all sterilizing filtration not exceed 8 hours, regardless of the product's bioburden or endotoxin
options.D: To avoid accumulation of filter extractables, which is the only reason for filtration time limits

questions.explanation: Total filtration time should be limited to an established maximum to prevent microorganisms from penetrating the filter and to avoid a significant increase in upstream bioburden and endotoxin. An upstream filter used for clarification or particulate removal, because it can become a substrate to which microorganisms attach, should also have a maximum use time that is set and justified. The document specifies no fixed 8 hours, and a time limit should be supported by data.

questions.question: Which statement about the number and frequency of media fills complies with the guidance?

options.A: One successful run at initial validation is enough, then once a year for each line
options.B: Two consecutive successful runs at initial validation, then once a quarter for each line
options.C: Three consecutive successful runs at initial validation, then only when the process changes
options.D: At least three consecutive successful runs at initial validation, then once every six months for each line

questions.explanation: For initial line qualification, at least three consecutive separate and successful runs are recommended, followed by routine requalification every six months for each line, with the design including representative activities across shifts and shift changes. All personnel authorized to enter the aseptic processing room during production (including technicians and maintenance staff) should participate in a media fill at least once a year. Changes and abnormal events are assessed separately through change control to decide whether additional runs are needed.

questions.question: Which statement is correct about bacterial retention validation of a 0.2 µm sterilizing filter?

options.A: B. diminuta is commonly used, with a challenge generally of at least 10⁷ organisms per cm² of effective filtration area, with no passage allowed
options.B: E. coli is commonly used, with a challenge generally of 10³ organisms per cm² of effective filtration area, with a small amount of passage tolerated
options.C: B. diminuta is commonly used, with a challenge only as high as the actual production bioburden, with no additional safety margin needed
options.D: Only bioburden isolates may be used, and B. diminuta is no longer suitable because its size is too large

questions.explanation: B. diminuta (ATCC 19146) has a mean diameter of about 0.3 µm and is the commonly used challenge organism for 0.2 µm filters. The challenge is generally at least 10⁷ organisms per cm² of effective filtration area, and the result must show no passage; this concentration provides a safety margin well above what production is expected to see. A bioburden isolate may be substituted only if shown to be equivalent or better.

questions.question: A media fill run filled 8,000 units, and 1 unit was found contaminated after incubation. According to the criteria recommended in the guidance, how should this be handled?

options.A: It is within the acceptable range; record it and close it out with no further action
options.B: Revalidation is required directly, with no investigation needed first
options.C: An investigation should be conducted, and repeating the media fill should be considered
options.D: The contamination rate is below 0.1%, so the run is considered acceptable and no investigation is needed

questions.explanation: When 5,000-10,000 units are filled, 1 contaminated unit should be investigated, with repeating the media fill considered; 2 contaminated units, after investigation, are considered cause for revalidation. When fewer than 5,000 units are filled, 1 contaminated unit is cause for revalidation. Any contaminated unit should be regarded as objectionable, investigated, and identified to species, and a low percentage cannot be used to consider the run acceptable.

questions.question: If media fill units are incubated at two temperatures, which statement complies with the guidance?

options.A: 7 days in total, 3-4 days at each temperature, high temperature first and then low
options.B: Not less than 14 days in total, with at least 7 days first at the higher temperature
options.C: Not less than 14 days in total, with temperatures adjustable between 15 and 40 °C as needed
options.D: Not less than 14 days in total, at least 7 days at each temperature, starting with the lower temperature

questions.explanation: Incubation should be not less than 14 days; when two temperatures are used, each should be for at least 7 days, starting with the lower temperature. The incubation temperature should never fall outside 20-35 °C and should be maintained within ±2.5 °C of the target.

questions.question: When should product-contact critical surfaces be sampled microbiologically, and how should a positive result be viewed?

options.A: Sample at the end of the aseptic operation; a positive result does not necessarily mean the batch must be rejected, but it must be investigated
options.B: Sample before filling starts; any positive result requires the batch to be rejected immediately
options.C: Sample every hour during filling; with a positive result, stop the line until the result turns negative
options.D: Sterilized surfaces need not be sampled, as long as there are sterilization records

questions.explanation: Critical surfaces should be sampled at the end of the aseptic operation, to avoid contacting sterilized surfaces during the process. Finding microorganisms at a critical site does not necessarily lead to rejection, but it should prompt an investigation of the operational information and data, with the awareness that a small number of false positives are possible. These surfaces should remain sterile throughout the operation, so they still need to be monitored.

questions.question: This month's average EM result for a room is below the action level, but one location exceeded the action level. According to the guidance, how should this be viewed?

options.A: Interpreting by the monthly average is enough; an acceptable average means the environment is in control
options.B: Only two consecutive excursions constitute a trend, and a single excursion can be ignored
options.C: Each result must be compared individually, because averaging can mask localized problems; a single excursion must still be evaluated
options.D: Any single excursion above the action level means every batch produced in that period must be rejected

questions.explanation: Each sample result should be compared individually with the alert/action level, because averaging can mask unacceptable localized conditions. Even without an adverse trend, a single result exceeding the action level should trigger an evaluation and a decision on whether remedial action is needed. Consecutive positives are only one kind of adverse trend, and a rising incidence of contamination is equally or more important; the document also does not say that a single excursion always means rejection.

questions.question: Which statement about the sporicidal agent in a disinfectant program is correct?

options.A: 70% IPA is effective against Bacillus spores, so a separate sporicidal agent is not needed
options.B: It should be used on a written schedule, and also when EM data show spore-forming organisms
options.C: As long as the routine disinfectant is effective against vegetative environmental organisms, the sporicidal agent is optional
options.D: It is started only after EM detects spore-forming organisms, and need not be scheduled in normal times

questions.explanation: Many commonly used disinfectants are not effective against spores; for example, 70% IPA is ineffective against spores of Bacillus spp. A sound disinfection program therefore includes a sporicidal agent, used on a written schedule and also when EM data show spore-forming organisms. Using it only after detection, or relying only on disinfectants effective against vegetative organisms, does not match the document.

questions.question: Which set of EM media incubation conditions is consistent with the guidance's description?

options.A: Total aerobic at 20-25 °C for 5-7 days; yeast/mold at 30-35 °C for 48-72 hours
options.B: Both total aerobic and yeast/mold at 30-35 °C for 14 days
options.C: Total aerobic at 30-35 °C for 24 hours; yeast/mold at 20-25 °C for 48 hours
options.D: Total aerobic at 30-35 °C for 48-72 hours; yeast/mold at 20-25 °C for 5-7 days

questions.explanation: The total aerobic bacterial count can be obtained by incubating at 30-35 °C for 48-72 hours; the combined yeast and mold count is generally obtained by incubating at 20-25 °C for 5-7 days. The pairing of "total aerobic at 20-25 °C, yeast/mold at 30-35 °C" swaps the two; 14 days is the media fill incubation time; and times of 24 and 48 hours are too short. EM media should also be confirmed to detect molds and bacteria, and each prepared lot of medium should undergo growth promotion.

questions.question: Which statement about identification of EM isolates complies with the guidance?

options.A: Biochemical or phenotypic methods can be used routinely; genotypic methods are more accurate and especially suited to failure investigations
options.B: All isolates must be identified by genotypic methods only, and biochemical methods are no longer accepted
options.C: For the critical area, a Gram stain is enough, with no identification to genus or species needed
options.D: Isolates from lower-control areas such as ISO 8 need no identification at all, only enumeration

questions.explanation: Genotypic methods are more accurate and precise than traditional biochemical and phenotypic methods and are especially suited to sterility test or media fill failure investigations, but routine identification may use appropriate biochemical and phenotypic methods. Critical area, surrounding area, and personnel monitoring should routinely identify to species (to genus where appropriate); supporting areas such as ISO 8 should also frequently be identified to species or genus, to build an effective in-house database of contaminants and detect species shifts early.

questions.question: A lot of 10,000 units has a contamination rate of 0.1%, and 20 units are used for the sterility test. According to the guidance's example, what is the approximate probability that the lot passes the test?

options.A: About 2%
options.B: About 50%
options.C: About 98%
options.D: About 90%

questions.explanation: The document gives the example that a lot of 10,000 units with 0.1% contamination tested with 20 units has about a 98% chance of passing the sterility test. USP statistics also indicate that the sampling plan detects contamination only about nine times out of ten when 10% of units are contaminated. The sterility test therefore has limited sensitivity, and any positive result is a serious CGMP problem.

questions.question: The initial sterility test result is positive. Under what circumstances may the result be declared invalid and the test repeated?

options.A: As long as the retest result is negative, the batch can be released on the retest result
options.B: Only when definitive documented evidence shows the contamination came from the testing process
options.C: Whenever the laboratory's past record of testing errors has been rather poor
options.D: Retest twice first, and if both are negative, the initial result can be declared invalid

questions.explanation: When microbial growth is observed, the batch should be considered non-sterile and an investigation started. Retesting is permitted only when the growth can be clearly attributed to laboratory error and definitive documented evidence shows the contamination occurred during testing; when the evidence is uncertain the batch should be rejected. A poor laboratory record cannot automatically be blamed either, and "release after retesting to a negative" is exactly what the document seeks to avoid.

questions.question: When investigating a positive sterility test, how should the laboratory's past error record be used?

options.A: When the laboratory record is poor, it is reasonable to presume that the contamination came mainly from the laboratory
options.B: When the laboratory record is good, it should be presumed that the contamination came from the sampling process rather than production
options.C: The laboratory record is unrelated to the investigation and should not be considered
options.D: A good record can lower suspicion of the laboratory, but a poor record cannot be used to presume the laboratory was the cause

questions.explanation: A good laboratory error record can reduce suspicion of the laboratory, because the contamination is more likely to have come from production. The reverse does not hold: when the record is poor, contamination should not be automatically attributed to the laboratory while real production problems are ignored. Every positive must therefore be thoroughly investigated.

questions.question: At which points in time should sterility test samples be taken to represent the whole batch and the state of the process?

options.A: At the beginning, middle, and end of the aseptic operation, and when interventions or deviations occur
options.B: Randomly at the end of filling only, to avoid interfering with filling operations
options.C: Only from the first tray of each shift, because that is the highest-risk period
options.D: By QC at its convenience, as long as the number meets USP requirements

questions.explanation: Samples should represent the whole batch and the state of the process, so they should be taken at the beginning, middle, and end of the aseptic operation, as well as in conjunction with process interventions or deviation events. Sampling at a single point in time or at convenience cannot represent the whole batch.

questions.question: Which statement about stoppages, interventions, and power failures in aseptic processing batch records complies with the guidance?

options.A: A brief power outage of less than one minute is normal fluctuation and need not be written in the batch record
options.B: Stoppages and unplanned interventions should be recorded with time and duration; a power outage that may affect quality is a deviation
options.C: Interventions need only be recorded by number, with times and content kept separately in the equipment's alarm log
options.D: EM and HVAC data are facility records and are outside the scope of batch release review

questions.explanation: Stoppages and unplanned interventions should be recorded in the batch record with the time of occurrence and duration, and interventions such as machine adjustments and repairs should be recorded in more detail than minor events. Any power outage that could affect quality, however brief, is a manufacturing deviation and must be entered in the batch record. EM data, personnel monitoring, and data on supporting systems (HEPA/HVAC, WFI, steam) are all necessary elements of release decisions.

questions.question: How should the classification of the environment surrounding an aseptic processing isolator be determined?

options.A: The inside of the isolator is already ISO 5, so it may be placed in an unclassified room
options.B: The surroundings must always be ISO 5, the same as the inside
options.C: The surroundings must always be ISO 7, which is a mandatory requirement for isolators
options.D: It depends on the design of the transfer interface and the number of transfers; ISO 8 is commonly used, and it should not be placed in an unclassified room

questions.explanation: The inside of an isolator should meet Class 100 (ISO 5). The classification of the surrounding environment depends on the design of the interface (such as the transfer port) and the number of transfers into and out of the isolator, with a Class 100,000 (ISO 8) background commonly used; an aseptic processing isolator should not be placed in an unclassified room. The document does not require the surroundings to be always ISO 5 or ISO 7.

questions.question: In an isolator, when decontamination is used to leave some product-contact surfaces free of viable organisms, what log reduction should be demonstrated with BIs, at a minimum?

options.A: At least 6-log
options.B: At least 4-log
options.C: At least 3-log
options.D: At least 12-log

questions.explanation: When decontamination is used for product-contact surfaces, at least a 6-log reduction should be demonstrated with an appropriate BI. For decontamination of general isolator interior surfaces, 4-6 logs can typically be justified depending on the application; the 4-log example applies to controlled, low-bioburden materials introduced via a transfer isolator (such as wrapped sterile items). 12 logs is the definition of overkill sterilization. Heat-resistant materials should be treated by heat sterilization such as SIP.

questions.question: In a blow-fill-seal operation, which three steps are most exposed to particulate contamination or the surrounding air?

options.A: Heating the resin, extruding the parison, and inflating the parison with sterile air to the shape of the mold
options.B: Filling the drug solution, sealing, and visual inspection after demolding
options.C: Cutting the parison, moving it under the mandrel, and removing the mandrel before sealing
options.D: Extruding the parison, filling the drug solution, and SIP sterilization of the equipment

questions.explanation: The three steps most exposed in most BFS operations are: (1) cutting the parison, (2) moving the parison under the blow-fill mandrel, and (3) removing the mandrel before sealing. The BFS surrounding environment is generally at least ISO 8, the critical area should meet the ISO 5 microbial standard during operation, and the exposure steps should use HEPA- or membrane-filtered sterile air.

questions.topic: Cell therapy release before sterility result
questions.question: Cell therapy products are often administered to patients before sterility test results are available. According to Appendix 3, how should this be supplemented?

options.A: Terminally sterilize the final product, so there is no need to wait for the sterility test
options.B: Consider adding a sterility test at an intermediate stage, and complete tests such as Gram stain and endotoxin before release
options.C: As long as a closed system is used throughout the process, all pre-release microbial and endotoxin tests can be waived
options.D: Delay administration until the 14-day sterility test result is available, with no exceptions

questions.explanation: Cell therapy products cannot be sterilized by filtration, so the entire process requires aseptic operation, and closed systems should be used where possible. If the final sterility result will not be available before administration, additional controls and tests should be considered, such as a sterility test at an intermediate stage (for example, after the last manipulation before harvest); microscopic examination, Gram stain (or other bacterial/fungal staining), and endotoxin testing should be completed before release and meet acceptance criteria.

questions.question: According to the guidance glossary, what is the definition of an overkill sterilization process?

options.A: A process achieving at least a 6-log reduction of microorganisms with a D value of at least 1 minute
options.B: Sterilization at 121 °C for more than twice the minimum validated time
options.C: A process achieving at least a 12-log reduction of microorganisms with a D value of at least 1 minute
options.D: A sterilization process achieving an SAL of 10⁻³ for any microorganism

questions.explanation: An overkill sterilization process is one sufficient to provide at least a 12-log reduction of microorganisms having a D value of at least 1 minute. The D value is the time in minutes at a specified temperature to reduce a specified microbial population by 1 log (90%). 6 logs is not the definition of overkill; "twice the time" is not the document's wording; and Section IX.C requires sterilization processes to demonstrate an SAL of 10⁻⁶ or better, not 10⁻³.
questions.reference: FDA Aseptic Guidance 2004 Glossary(Overkill sterilization process, D value)
